fields.hypothesis: Integrate an ultrasonic vibration treatment during melting and pouring (ultrasonic-assisted casting) to promote finer, uniformly interconnected lamellar colony formation, thereby reducing internal stress concentrations and enhancing both strength and room-temperature ductility.
fields.material_initial_state: Eutectic HEA as produced by conventional casting, characterized by dual-phase lamellar colonies with variable spacing and suboptimal interconnectivity at internal boundaries that facilitate microcrack initiation.
fields.intervention: Introduce high-intensity ultrasonic vibrations into the melt during the casting process to induce cavitation and acoustic streaming.
fields.conditions: Ultrasonic frequency and power must be optimized such that cavitation promotes increased nucleation and refined lamellar spacing without disrupting the overall dual-phase equilibrium. The treatment should be applied during the liquid state prior to solidification when the melt is sufficiently fluid.
fields.structural_mediator: Ultrasonic vibrations refine the nucleation process and promote a more uniform and finer lamellar colony spacing, which increases the interfacial area in a controlled manner. This uniformity reduces localized stress concentrations and creates a more continuous, cohesive microstructure.
fields.mechanism: The mechanism relies on the well-known phenomenon where ultrasonic energy in a melt induces cavitation (bubble formation and collapse) and acoustic streaming, leading to enhanced nucleation and homogenization of the microstructure. A refined and uniformly connected lamellar structure can better distribute the deformation-induced stresses and thus delay the onset of microcrack nucleation—all while preserving the transformation-induced plasticity (TRIP) behavior observed in dual-phase HEAs (PMC5701024::web::004::microstructure_evolution_after_fsp).
fields.predicted_outcome: Ultrasonic-assisted cast samples are expected to show a statistically significant reduction in average lamellar spacing with a more uniform colony orientation. In tensile tests, these samples should manifest improvements in both yield/ultimate tensile strengths and uniform elongation compared to those produced by conventional casting. The size of the effect is uncertain but should be measurable.
fields.baseline: Conventional casting of the eutectic HEA which results in a relatively heterogeneous lamellar colony structure with non-uniform spacing and connectivity, leading to stress concentration and early microcrack formation.
fields.boundary: The ultrasonic treatment parameters must be precisely controlled; excessive ultrasonic energy could lead to undesirable porosity or upset the delicate balance between the dual phases, while insufficient energy would not yield the desired refinement.
fields.uncertainty: The quantitative influence of ultrasonic-assisted casting on lamellar colony refinement and subsequent tensile improvements is uncertain and subject to experimental calibration.

falsification_experiment.design: Cast two sets of eutectic HEA samples: one using standard casting and another using identical conditions but with ultrasonic vibration during casting. Characterize the microstructure (lamellar spacing, colony uniformity) using SEM/EBSD, and perform room-temperature tensile tests.
measurements: Lamellar spacing and colony uniformity via SEM/EBSD
Yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and uniform elongation from tensile tests
Fracture surface analysis to detect microcrack initiation sites
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ultrasonic-assisted cast samples do not demonstrate a significant refinement and homogenization of lamellar colonies along with corresponding improvements in both strength and ductility compared to the conventional cast samples, the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C14
pool.builds_on: The finding from the paper that the microstructure plays a crucial role in controlling mechanical properties and the known benefits of controlled microstructural orientations.
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis applies a directional solidification approach specifically to eutectic HEAs to control lamellar colony alignment — an intervention not covered in the paper — to mitigate the inherent brittleness of the dual-phase lamellar colonies by reducing microcrack initiation.

fields.hypothesis: Directional solidification will align the lamellar colonies along the tensile loading axis, reducing deleterious misorientation of internal boundaries and mitigating microcrack initiation, thereby simultaneously enhancing both strength and ductility.
fields.material_initial_state: A conventional eutectic high-entropy alloy with dual-phase, randomly oriented lamellar colonies that exhibit microcrack initiation at misoriented phase boundaries during room-temperature tensile deformation.
fields.intervention: Process the alloy via directional solidification using a high thermal gradient and controlled growth conditions to produce a strong preferential alignment of lamellar colonies with the tensile axis.
fields.conditions: Directional solidification parameters must be chosen to yield a fine lamellar spacing (e.g., sub-micron scale) with an alignment within ±10° of the tensile axis; cooling rates should be optimized to avoid coarsening.
fields.structural_mediator: Aligned lamellar colonies leading to continuous and uniformly oriented internal phase boundaries that reduce local stress concentrations.
fields.mechanism: Aligning the lamellae with the loading direction minimizes the misorientation between adjacent colonies, thus reducing the number of stress concentration sites that serve as crack initiation points. The aligned microstructure also maintains effective barriers to dislocation motion, preserving strength via a refined microstructure.
fields.predicted_outcome: Compared to the unmodified, randomly oriented baseline, the alloy should exhibit an increase in both tensile yield strength and room-temperature ductility. (The approximate magnitude is uncertain, but improvements are expected if alignment is within the target tolerance.)
fields.baseline: Eutectic HEAs with dual-phase lamellar colonies formed via conventional processing that show premature microcracking during tensile deformation.
fields.boundary: The improvement is contingent on achieving a high degree of lamellar alignment without introducing detrimental segregation or grain coarsening. The effect is expected to hold under room-temperature tensile deformation conditions with fine-scale (sub–micron) lamellae.
fields.uncertainty: Precise quantitative improvements are uncertain without optimizing the solidification parameters, and the sensitivity to residual misorientation remains to be fully established.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of specimens: one manufactured via conventional processing with random lamellar orientation and the other via directional solidification yielding aligned lamellae. Conduct room-temperature tensile tests and microstructural analysis (e.g., EBSD) to assess lamellar alignment.
measurements: Degree of lamellar alignment (misorientation angle distribution by EBSD)
Tensile yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and total elongation in room-temperature tensile tests
Fractography to assess microcrack initiation sites
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the directionally solidified samples do not show a statistically significant improvement in both tensile strength and ductility (or if microcrack initiation remains comparable to the baseline) despite a confirmed lamellar alignment improvement, then the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C15
pool.builds_on: The general understanding that recovery annealing can relieve residual stresses and heal interfacial defects in metallic materials.
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis introduces a post-deformation, low-temperature annealing step for eutectic HEAs to target internal lamellar boundary healing — a single processing intervention not explored in the paper — aiming to improve ductility without sacrificing strength.

fields.hypothesis: A short-time, low-temperature post-deformation (recovery) annealing treatment will facilitate stress relief and interface healing at the lamellar colony boundaries, reducing microcrack nucleation while preserving the fine microstructure responsible for high strength.
fields.material_initial_state: A eutectic HEA exhibiting dual-phase lamellar colonies produced via standard processing that is prone to microcracking during room-temperature tensile deformation due to high internal residual stresses and sharp, non-equilibrated boundaries.
fields.intervention: Apply a carefully controlled annealing treatment at an intermediate temperature (e.g., 300–400 °C) for a brief duration (e.g., 5–15 minutes) after primary processing to promote localized recovery without significant coarsening.
fields.conditions: The treatment temperature must remain well below the recrystallization temperature to prevent microstructural coarsening, and the time must be short enough to allow stress relief at phase boundaries while preserving the fine lamellar spacing.
fields.structural_mediator: Reduction of localized residual stresses and slight atomic diffusion at the lamellar interfaces, resulting in more coherent or slightly ‘healed’ boundaries that resist crack initiation.
fields.mechanism: Sub-recrystallization annealing leads to recovery processes, such as dislocation rearrangement and limited atomic diffusion, which can relieve stress concentrations at the internal boundaries of the lamellae. Improved interface coherency reduces the propensity for microcracking while maintaining the nanoscale barrier structure that underpins high strength.
fields.predicted_outcome: The treated alloy should exhibit enhanced tensile ductility (i.e., higher elongation) with minimal reduction in yield strength compared to the untreated baseline, though the exact magnitude requires experimental confirmation.
fields.baseline: Eutectic HEAs with dual-phase lamellar microstructures produced without post-deformation recovery annealing, which show premature microcrack formation during tensile deformation.
fields.boundary: The process window must ensure that the annealing temperature and time are low enough to avoid undesirable phase coarsening or microstructural transformation that could compromise strength.
fields.uncertainty: The exact annealing window for optimal recovery without coarsening is not precisely known and may vary with alloy composition and prior processing conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Process samples using conventional route to form the eutectic lamellar microstructure and then subject a subset to the proposed recovery annealing treatment. Characterize the microstructure (TEM/EBSD) to verify interface changes and perform tensile tests at room temperature.
measurements: Tensile stress-strain curves comparing yield strength and elongation
Residual stress mapping (e.g., XRD or microdiffraction) near lamellar boundaries
Microstructural analysis to check for any coarsening
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the low-temperature annealed samples do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in tensile ductility without a detrimental drop in yield strength compared to the untreated baseline, or if significant coarsening is observed, the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C16
pool.builds_on: Established knowledge from NiAl systems showing that trace additions of Boron improve boundary cohesion and ductility.
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis integrates a microalloying strategy with Boron addition into eutectic HEAs—a single compositional intervention not explored in the paper—to improve the internal boundary cohesion and thereby enhance both strength and room-temperature ductility.

fields.hypothesis: Introducing a trace amount (e.g., ~0.1 at%) of Boron during alloy synthesis will lead to its segregation at the internal lamellar boundaries, enhancing interfacial cohesion and mitigating microcrack initiation while simultaneously contributing to solid solution strengthening.
fields.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloy with dual-phase lamellar colonies exhibiting numerous internal boundaries that promote microcrack initiation during room-temperature tensile deformation.
fields.intervention: Modify the alloy composition by adding a minute amount of Boron during melting and casting, ensuring a homogeneous distribution that promotes segregation of Boron to the internal boundaries during subsequent thermomechanical processing.
fields.conditions: The Boron content should be carefully controlled (e.g., around 0.1 at%) to avoid formation of brittle boride phases and must be processed under conditions that allow for its preferential segregation (potentially assisted by a suitable cooling rate or secondary heat treatment).
fields.structural_mediator: Boron segregation at the internal lamellar boundaries lowers the boundary energy and enhances interfacial strength, reducing the likelihood of microcrack nucleation under tensile stress.
fields.mechanism: Boron is known in NiAl-based systems to improve ductility by reducing the energy of anti-phase boundaries and strengthening grain boundaries. In this eutectic HEA, the segregated Boron will bond at the lamellar interfaces, increasing cohesion and resistance to crack propagation while also providing minor solid solution strengthening effects.
fields.predicted_outcome: Relative to the Boron-free baseline, the Boron-doped alloy is expected to show improved room-temperature tensile ductility (increased elongation) together with maintaining or slightly enhancing tensile strength. The magnitude of improvement is uncertain and must be determined experimentally.
fields.baseline: Eutectic HEAs processed conventionally without any microalloying additions, which display limited tensile ductility due to microcrack initiation at internal boundaries.
fields.boundary: The beneficial effects are expected only if Boron segregates to the lamellar boundaries without forming discontinuous brittle boride precipitates; too high a concentration or inappropriate processing may negate these benefits.
fields.uncertainty: The precise level of Boron segregation and its quantitative impact on mechanical properties remain to be experimentally established.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two batches of the eutectic HEA: one with the standard composition and one with ~0.1 at% Boron addition. Process both under identical thermomechanical conditions and perform detailed microstructural analysis (e.g., atom probe tomography and TEM) to assess Boron segregation, along with identical room-temperature tensile tests.
measurements: Microstructural characterization to confirm Boron segregation at lamellar boundaries
Tensile stress-strain curves to compare yield strength and ductility
Fractography to assess differences in crack initiation and propagation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Boron-doped alloy does not show a statistically significant improvement in ductility and strength, or if brittle boride phases form that degrade performance, the hypothesis is falsified.

top3.label: C7
top3.builds_on: the finding that nano-precipitation (ordered L12) can enhance strength via Orowan dislocation bowing while retaining ductility, as described in PMC6478865.
top3.what_is_new: This hypothesis proposes a compositional modification (minor Zr doping) aimed at specifically enhancing interfacial cohesion and generating interfacial obstacles—targeting the colony boundaries where microcrack initiation occurs—rather than reprecipitating within the fcc phase.

fields.hypothesis: Minor Zr doping will promote segregation at the lamellar colony boundaries in the Al0.7CoCrFeNi eutectic HEA, thereby simultaneously enhancing interfacial cohesion to delay microcrack nucleation and inducing additional nanoscale obstacles for dislocation motion to raise strength.
fields.material_initial_state: Eutectic HEA Al0.7CoCrFeNi with dual-phase lamellar colonies (fcc + B2) produced by conventional melting, homogenization, and rolling.
fields.intervention: Introduce a minor amount (e.g., 0.5–1 at.%) of Zr during alloy melting.
fields.conditions: Maintain the same thermo-mechanical processing (homogenization at ~1150 °C, cold rolling, brief annealing) while incorporating the dopant; Zr is expected to segregate during solidification and subsequent heat-treatment.
fields.structural_mediator: Zr-enriched layers or nanoscale Zr-rich precipitates at fcc/B2 interphase boundaries.
fields.mechanism: Zr has a high tendency to segregate to interfaces, which can increase the bonding strength and reduce stress concentrations at the colony boundaries. This results in fewer sites for crack initiation under tensile loading while the Zr-rich nanoscale precipitates act as additional obstacles to dislocation motion (via Orowan-like mechanisms), contributing to increased yield strength without sacrificing ductility.
fields.predicted_outcome: An alloy with improved tensile yield strength (potentially on the order of a 10–15% increase) and enhanced room-temperature ductility relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline.
fields.baseline: The standard Al0.7CoCrFeNi eutectic HEA with lamellar fcc + B2 microstructure processed without additional alloying elements.
fields.boundary: The beneficial effect is expected if Zr content remains low; excessive Zr may lead to formation of continuous brittle intermetallic films. The effectiveness depends on the segregation kinetics during processing, so processing parameters must be maintained to favor interface enrichment.
fields.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of strength and ductility enhancement is uncertain without experimental calibration, and the stability of Zr segregation under prolonged stress remains to be evaluated.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Al0.7CoCrFeNi alloys – one with 0.5–1 at.% Zr addition and a control with no Zr. Process both identically according to the conventional route (melting, homogenization, rolling, and annealing). Perform microstructural analysis (e.g., TEM/EDS) to verify Zr segregation at lamellar boundaries and then conduct room-temperature tensile tests.
measurements: Tensile yield strength
Ultimate tensile strength
Elongation to failure
Microstructural characterization of interface chemistry
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Zr-doped alloy does not exhibit both a statistically significant increase in yield strength and an improvement (or at least no degradation) in tensile ductility compared to the control, or if no Zr segregation is observed at the boundaries, then the hypothesis is falsified.

top3.label: C1
top3.builds_on: the finding that nanostructural dual heterogeneities, including the presence of nano-precipitates, contribute to enhanced back-stress strengthening and ductility in processed EHEAs (PMC6687781).
top3.what_is_new: This hypothesis proposes, rather than using a complex hybrid deformation route, a controlled thermal post-treatment specifically designed to engineer the colony boundaries via nanoprecipitation, a route not explored in the paper.

fields.hypothesis: A short low-temperature annealing treatment designed to induce the formation of coherent nanoprecipitates at the lamellar colony boundaries will improve both strength and room‐temperature tensile ductility.
fields.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) with dual-phase lamellar colonies containing L12 and B2 phases, as typically produced by conventional processing (as‐cast or cryo‐rolling with minimal post‐annealing).
fields.intervention: Expose the alloy to a brief isothermal anneal (e.g., around 500 °C for a few minutes) immediately after processing to promote solute segregation and nucleation of nanoscale precipitates at the internal boundaries.
fields.conditions: The annealing temperature and time must be selected to ensure that nanoprecipitate formation is promoted at colony interfaces without causing bulk coarsening; the treatment should remain below temperatures that trigger excessive phase coarsening.
fields.structural_mediator: Formation of coherent nanoprecipitates along the lamellar boundaries that reinforce the interfaces.
fields.mechanism: The newly formed nanoprecipitates enhance the local strength by impeding dislocation motion and increasing the cohesion at the internal boundaries. This reduces stress concentration and microcrack initiation while also generating geometrically necessary dislocations that promote back-stress strengthening, thus delaying necking and failure.
fields.predicted_outcome: Relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, the alloy is expected to exhibit a modest to significant increase in yield strength and ultimate tensile strength (on the order of 10–20% improvements, subject to optimization) with a simultaneous improvement in uniform elongation.
fields.baseline: As-processed EHEA with conventional or hybrid-rolling routes showing dual-phase lamellar colonies and room-temperature brittleness initiated at internal boundaries.
fields.boundary: The treatment must be carefully controlled so that the anneal is not too long or too hot (which could lead to unwanted grain growth or coarsening of the lamellar structure) and must be applied to alloys with the typical eutectic colony makeup.
fields.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of the mechanical property improvements is uncertain and will depend on the exact annealing parameters chosen.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of EHEA samples under identical processing conditions. Subject one set to the proposed low-temperature annealing treatment while keeping the other set as the baseline. Perform detailed TEM characterization to confirm nanoprecipitate formation at lamellar boundaries and carry out room-temperature tensile tests.
measurements: TEM imaging and selected area diffraction (to assess precipitate formation and interfacial structure)
Stress-strain tensile tests (to measure yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and uniform elongation)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not show evidence of nanoprecipitate formation at the colony interfaces, or if the mechanical properties (strength and ductility) are not statistically better than or are inferior to the baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

top3.label: C5

top3.what_is_new: This hypothesis introduces a compositional modification (Mo addition) to further stabilize and refine the B2 phase at lamellar interfaces, a strategy not discussed in the paper, thereby assessing its potential to synergistically improve strength and ductility.

fields.hypothesis: Introduce a minor molybdenum (Mo) addition into the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA to promote the formation of uniformly refined, Mo-stabilized B2 precipitates at lamellar boundaries, improving both strength and ductility.
fields.material_initial_state: Standard AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA with dual-phase lamellar colonies formed by casting, cold-rolling, and annealing, where B2 phases already exist but without Mo stabilization.
fields.intervention: Modify the alloy composition by substituting a small fraction (e.g., 2–3 at%) of one of the base elements (such as Fe or Cr) with Mo.
fields.conditions: The modified alloy should be processed with the same thermo-mechanical treatment (cold-rolling and annealing) as the baseline to isolate the chemical composition effect. The Mo content must be kept low enough to avoid formation of large, brittle intermetallic compounds.
fields.structural_mediator: A refined dispersion of Mo-stabilized B2 precipitates along lamellar interfaces, leading to more coherent and stronger interphase boundaries.
fields.mechanism: Mo is known to refine and stabilize intermetallic phases (e.g., in NiAl systems) by lowering the nucleation barrier for fine precipitate formation. In the lamellar architecture of EHEAs, the Mo-modified B2 precipitates can better constrain dislocation motion and absorb local deformation, thus boosting back-stress hardening and impeding microcrack propagation. This intervention builds on the paper's observation that the B2 phase contributes to strengthening and ductility through back-stress effects.
fields.predicted_outcome: The alloy with Mo addition should exhibit higher yield strength and improved uniform elongation compared to the baseline alloy. Although the magnitude of improvement is not precisely known, both properties are expected to increase under the same processing conditions.
fields.baseline: The original AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy processed without Mo addition, exhibiting an inherited lamellar structure with B2 and FCC phases.
fields.boundary: The beneficial effect is expected only with minor Mo additions; excess Mo could lead to coarse or continuous brittle intermetallic films. The improvement is relevant under room-temperature tensile loading conditions.
fields.uncertainty: The optimal Mo content and the precise effect on precipitate size distribution and interfacial strength requires experimental optimization.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloys: one with the standard AlCoCrFeNi2.1 composition and one with a 2–3 at% Mo substitution under identical processing conditions. Conduct comprehensive microstructural characterization and room-temperature tensile tests.
